intro: Chapter 4 of 1 Nephi is the climax of the brass-plates story. Nephi rallies his frightened, murmuring brothers with the example of Moses and the Red Sea, and they return once more to the walls of Jerusalem. Under cover of night Nephi creeps alone into the city and finds Laban fallen to the ground, drunk with wine. Drawing Laban's own sword, Nephi is constrained by the Spirit to slay him — and the chapter dwells at length on Nephi's inner struggle before he obeys, reasoning that it is better that one man perish than that a whole nation dwindle in unbelief. Nephi then dons Laban's clothing and armor, impersonates him with Laban's own voice, and commands Laban's servant, Zoram, to bring the brass plates out of the treasury. Leading Zoram toward the city walls, the ruse nearly unravels when Nephi's brothers, taking him for Laban, flee in terror; Nephi calls out and reveals himself. Zoram in turn tries to flee, but Nephi — a physically large and strong man — restrains him and swears an oath that Zoram shall be a free man if he joins them in the wilderness. Zoram takes his own oath to remain, and together they carry the plates and the servant back to the tent of Lehi.
reading_tip: This chapter weaves together several core grammar constructions, each introduced with the vocabulary below. The narrative frame `چنین گذشت که` (and it came to pass) opens most episodes. Watch the **subjunctive** (`بـ-` prefix, no `می-`) after `تا` (so that / in order to) and after `مگر اینکه` (unless), and the **imperative** forms `بنگر` (behold) and `بکُش` (slay). The **future tense** — `خواه-` + past-stem infinitive (`خواهند شد`, `خواهد بود`, `خواهی داشت`) — appears here for deliverance and promise. Possessive suffixes are unusually dense (`سرش` his head, `کمرم` my waist, `اربابش` his master, `شمشیرش` his sword), and the chapter closes on a cluster of **oath** idioms (`سوگند یاد کردن`, `به هستی سَروَر سوگند`). Compound verbs (`گمان کردن`, `نگه داشتن`, `بدست آوردن`, `فرمان بردن`) carry much of the action — parse the noun before `کردن`/`شدن`/`بردن` first. Read each verse's interlinear gloss before the English so the morphology, not the translation, drives your understanding.

forms.desc: Persian uses the Indo-Persian digits `۰ ۱ ۲ ۳ ۴ ۵ ۶ ۷ ۸ ۹` (not the Arabic–Western `0–9`). Each digit's pronunciation is introduced at first appearance in this chapter.

forms.note: Teens (11–19) and multiples of ten (20, 30 …) are independent Persian words, not digit-by-digit composites. Verse numbers count as first occurrences of each numeral.

entries.title: Grammar: The object marker را
entries.body: The particle `را` _rā_ marks a **definite direct object**. It follows the entire object noun phrase — after any ezafe chain, plural suffix, or possessive clitic — not the bare noun. In this chapter it repeatedly marks the object of the disguise-and-slaying narrative.

entries.meaning: so that, in order to (+ subjunctive); until; as far as

entries.title: Grammar: Subjunctive after تا
entries.body: `تا` _tā_ introduces a **purpose clause** ("so that, in order that") whose verb stands in the **subjunctive** — marked by the `بـ-` prefix and/or the subjunctive endings, and never by `می-`. `تا` also means "until" (with past indicative) and "as far as / inasmuch as."

examples.persian: تا به خانوادۀ لیحای در بیابان بپیوندد
examples.translit: tā be xānevāde-ye Liḥāy dar bīyābān be-peyvandad
examples.en: so that he might join the family of Lehi in the wilderness

examples.persian: سَروَر قادر است تا ما را رهایی دهد
examples.translit: Sarvar qāder ast tā mā rā rahāyī dehad

entries.title: Grammar: چنین گذشت که (and it came to pass)
entries.body: `چنین گذشت که` _čonīn gozašt ke_ — literally "thus it passed that" — renders the Book of Mormon formula **"and it came to pass."** It opens most episodes in the chapter. `چنین` "thus" + `گذشت` (past 3sg of `گذشتن` "to pass") + `که` complementizer.

examples.persian: و چنین گذشت که من به برادرانم سخن گفته، گفتم
examples.translit: o čonīn gozašt ke man be barādarān-am soxan gofte, goftam
examples.en: And it came to pass that I spake unto my brethren, saying

entries.meaning: to pass, go by; (time) to elapse

entries.title: Grammar: Possessive clitics -am -at -aš -mān -tān -šān
entries.body: Persian marks possession by attaching an **enclitic** directly to the noun: `-am` (my), `-at` (thy), `-aš` (his/her/its), `-mān` (our), `-tān` (your), `-šān` (their). The disguise scene turns on these: تracking whose sword, head, or waist is meant depends entirely on the ending. On a plural noun the clitic follows the plural suffix (`برادرانم` = برادر + ان + م).

examples.translit: barādarān-am
examples.en: my brethren

examples.translit: panǰāh nafar-aš
examples.en: his fifty

examples.en: the hair of his head

entries.title: Grammar: Compound (light-verb) verbs
entries.body: Persian forms most of its verbal vocabulary by combining a **noun or adjective** with a **light verb** — usually `کردن` (do), `شدن` (become), `دادن` (give), `گفتن` (say), `داشتن` (hold). The preceding element carries the meaning; the light verb carries the tense and person. This chapter is unusually dense with them: `سخن گفتن` (to speak), `نگه داشتن` (to keep), `بدست آوردن` (to obtain), `فرمان دادن` (to command), `غُرولند کردن` (to murmur), `سوگند یاد کردن` (to swear).

entries.title: Grammar: Comparative -تر and superlative -ترین
entries.body: The comparative is formed with the suffix **`-تر`** _-tar_ ("more, -er"), the superlative with **`-ترین`** _-tarīn_ ("most, -est"). The comparative is followed by `از` _az_ "than." These attach to adjectives directly: `توانا` "able" → `تواناتر` "mightier" → `تواناترین` "mightiest."

examples.translit: ū az hame-ye zamīn tavānā-tar ast

entries.title: Grammar: The indefinite suffix -ی (-ī)
entries.body: Indefiniteness ("a, an; a certain") is marked by the **enclitic `-ی`** _-ī_ on the noun. After a word ending in the vowel _-e_ (silent ه) it is written as a separate `ای`: `فرشته` "angel" → `فرشته ای` "an angel." On consonant-final nouns it attaches directly: `مردی` "a man," `نیازی` "a need," `سوگندی` "an oath."

examples.translit: ferešte-ī bar šomā soxan gofte ast
examples.en: an angel hath spoken unto you

examples.translit: mard-ī rā dīdam

entries.title: Grammar: Imperfective می- and its negation نمی-
entries.body: The prefix **`می-`** _mī-_ marks **imperfective aspect** — habitual, progressive, or present-tense action. Its negation is **`نمی-`** _nemī-_. In the Persian BoM source the prefix is written with a space before the stem, so `می` and the verb are separate tokens (the reader should read them as one word). The prefix is dropped in the subjunctive and (for `داشتن`) in the present indicative.

examples.persian: شما می دانید که این راست است
examples.translit: šomā mī-dānīd ke īn rāst ast
examples.en: ye know that this is true

entries.title: Grammar: Passive and inchoative شدن
entries.body: `شدن` _šodan_ "to become" serves as the **passive auxiliary**: a past participle (or a light-verb noun) + `شدن` yields "to be (done)." The same verb gives **inchoative** ("become X") readings with adjectives. This chapter uses it constantly: `راهنمایی می شدم` "I was being led," `وادار شدم` "I was constrained," `کنده کاری شده بود` "had been engraved," `غرق شدند` "were drowned," `راهی ... شدیم` "we set out."

entries.title: Grammar: Future tense (خواه- + past-stem infinitive)
entries.body: The **future tense** is formed with the present-stem auxiliary **`خواه-`** _xāh-_ (inflected for person) followed by the **short (past-stem) infinitive** of the main verb — the infinitive minus final `-ن`: `بود` (← `بودن`), `شد` (← `شدن`), `داشت` (← `داشتن`). The auxiliary takes **no** `بـ-` or `می-`. It usually renders "shall/will."

examples.translit: ānhā dar sarzamīn-e mowʿūd kāmravā xāhand šod
examples.en: they shall prosper in the land of promise

examples.persian: تو جایی با ما خواهی داشت
examples.translit: to jāyī bā mā xāhī dāšt
examples.en: thou shalt have a place with us

entries.title: Grammar: Archaic narrative suffix -ا (گفتا)
entries.body: The Book of Mormon Persian uses the archaic literary suffix **`-ا`** _-ā_ on a past-tense verb to mark **solemn narrative speech**: `گفتا` _goftā_ = "he said" (introducing quoted speech). This is a relic of classical Persian poetry and formal prose, not used in modern speech. It pairs here with other archaisms: the imperatives `بنگر`/`بنگرید` "behold," the affirmative `آری` "yea," and `سَروَر` "the Lord."

examples.persian: او در بیابان بر من گفت، گفتا که
examples.translit: ū dar bīyābān bar man goft, goftā ke
examples.en: he spake unto me in the wilderness, saying

entries.meaning: archaic narrative past 3sg of `گفتن`; see [Grammar: Archaic narrative suffix -ا](#grammar-archaic-narrative-suffix)

entries.title: Grammar: Subjunctive after مگر اینکه (unless)
entries.body: `مگر اینکه` _magar īnke_ "unless, except that" introduces a **conditional exception** whose verb stands in the **subjunctive**. Like `تا` and `اگر`, it triggers the `بـ-` prefix (or subjunctive endings) and blocks `می-`. Here the subjunctive is the perfect subjunctive `داشته باشند` "(unless) they should have."

examples.persian: مگر اینکه آنها قانون را داشته باشند
examples.translit: magar īnke ānhā qānūn rā dāšte bāšand
examples.en: save they should have the law
